Designing experiments for global rollout

Multi-arm designs for the GATE under partial interference

Molly Offer-Westort (Chicago) · Drew Dimmery (Hertie School)

2026-09-24

Tuning video playback at Meta

Buffering harder for one video starves the next, so configurations interfere. The decision is a single configuration, shipped to everyone.

Drawn mock, not a screenshot. Playback is governed by a long list of engineering parameters; the names here are illustrative: the real ones control pre-buffering, prefetch and abort behaviour, and are benign and invisible to the user. The metric we will use throughout is stalls, which are a bad user experience, so lower is better. Interference here is physical, not behavioural — it is the shared pipe.

Optimization needs a good model

The same intervention, similar measure, radically different ability to optimize.

  • User-level precision grows only with the user base
  • Finer grain splits the users you have
  • How fine can we go?

Right panel: Figure 6 of Letham, Karrer, Ottoni & Bakshy (2019), “Constrained Bayesian Optimization with Noisy Experiments,” Bayesian Analysis 14(2).

We care about rollout

Sessions \(j\), videos \(i\), arms \(A_{j,i} \in \{0,\ldots,M\}\) with \(0\) the control.

  • Partial interference: \(Y_{j,i}\) depends on the arms inside session \(j\) only.

Two questions about arm \(m\):

  1. what it does to switch for one video,
  2. or switch every video, for every user?
  • Only the second is shippable — the Global Average Treatment Effect:

\[\Psi_m^{\mathrm{GATE}} \;=\; \mathbb{E}\Big[\, \underbrace{Y_{j,i}(\bar{\mathbf m}_j)}_{\substack{\text{every video}\\ \text{on arm } m}} \;-\; \underbrace{Y_{j,i}(\bar{\mathbf 0}_j)}_{\substack{\text{every video}\\ \text{on control}}} \,\Big]\]

The first depends on the mix your experiment happened to create: a world nobody will live in.

Two standard designs, two problems

Bias for the GATE Precision
Cluster-uniform — all videos for a user/session get one arm Unbiased You have as many observations as users/sessions
Unit-level — each video assigned independently Biased Every video counts

They differ in one thing: the within-session treatment correlation \(\rho_T\): one, or zero.

Unit-level designs are precise for the wrong estimand: a “low-data” video is surrounded by a mixture.

Both problems are visible in the data

Cluster-uniform: ~3× the SEs. Unit-level: ~1.5× the effect magnitudes.

These designs exist in a continuum

Our work examines the middle column.

Why an endpoint is rarely optimal

Moulton (1986): correlated assignment inflates the variance by

\[1 + \hlblue{\rho_T}\,\hlred{\rho_u}\,(\hlgreen{\bar N} - 1)\]

It is a product: what the treatment correlation you impose costs is set by the outcome correlation you inherit. At \(\hlred{\rho_u} \approx 0\) it is free.

Bias runs the other way. So a good choice of \(\hlblue{\rho_T}\) depends on \(\hlred{\rho_u}\) and \(\hlgreen{\bar N}\).

One knob, not discrete choice

Per session, draw a mix over arms — 70% arm 3, 20% control, … — then assign each video from it:

\[\underbrace{\Pi_j \sim \mathrm{Dirichlet}(\bar\alpha,\ldots,\bar\alpha)}_{\text{one mix per session}}, \qquad \underbrace{\Pr\big[A_{j,i} = m \mid \Pi_j\big] = \Pi_j[m]}_{\text{videos i.i.d. given the mix}}\]

The whole design choice is one concentration parameter: \(\rho_T(\bar\alpha) = 1/[(M{+}1)\bar\alpha+1]\).

\(\bar\alpha \to 0\) interior \(\bar\alpha \to \infty\)
lopsided mixes, \(\rho_T \to 1\) anything in between balanced mixes, \(\rho_T \to 0\)
= cluster-uniform our work = unit-level

Smoothly varying design choices

The family embeds both standard designs as its endpoints.

The workflow

The pilot is exploratory: it picks a region of the dial, not the GATE.

Step 3 loops on itself at the same tuned \(\bar\alpha\) — that is where the optimization happens.

The workflow

Nothing here is specific to the GATE or to RMSE: swap the target contrast or the loss, and the machinery is unchanged.

Step 1: Pilot

One concurrent pilot, split across a few prespecified \(\bar\alpha\) so realized shares vary. Three outputs:

  1. the cluster size distribution \(\{N_j\}\): mean and variance
  2. the variance components: total variance \(\sigma^2 + \tau^2\), and the outcome correlation \(\rho_u = \tau^2/(\sigma^2+\tau^2)\)
  3. a parsimonious summary of interference

One modelling ingredient

How a video’s outcome responds to its own arm and to the mix around it, the realized shares \(p_{j[\ell]}\) of session \(j\) on arm \(\ell\):

\[\mathbb{E}\big[\,Y_{j,i} \,\big|\, A_{j,i} = m,\ \mathbf p_j\,\big] \;=\; \underbrace{\beta_m}_{\text{own arm}} \;+\; \underbrace{\textstyle\sum_{\ell} \delta_{m,\ell}\, p_{j[\ell]}}_{\substack{\text{linear in the shares}\\ \text{around you}}}\]

Under a uniform rollout \(p_{j[m]} = 1\), so

\[\Psi_m^{\mathrm{GATE}} \;=\; (\beta_m + \delta_{m,m}) - \beta_0\]

We are not asking this model for correct specification. It is a working model, used to calibrate a design.

\((M{+}1)^2\) mean parameters: 121 for our 10 treatment groups and control. For us: one slope, on the share of “high-data” videos.

Written out: E[Y | arm m, mix p] = beta_m + sum_l delta_{m,l} p_l, and GATE_m = (beta_m + delta_mm) - beta_0. The technical appendix gives the paper’s exposure proof, bias approximation, and replay implementation details. This is the multi-arm, clustered version of Baird et al. (2018) and Chin (2018).

Linear-in-means: Manski (1993); Bramoullé, Djebbari & Fortin (2009). Interference regressions: Chin (2018); Baird, Bohren, McIntosh & Özler (2018).

Step 2 — Tune

Score each candidate design by its expected RMSE, and take the argmin:

\[\bar\alpha^\star \;\in\; \arg\min_{\bar\alpha}\ \frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M}\Big\{\widehat{\mathrm{Bias}}_m(\bar\alpha)^2 + \widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_m(\bar\alpha)\Big\}^{1/2}\]

Bias — closed form

Substitute the pilot’s \(\widehat\delta\) into the exposure moments: \(\widehat{\mathrm{Bias}}_m\) is arithmetic in \((\widehat\delta,\ \bar\alpha,\ \{N_j\})\). No simulation.

Variance — design replay

Simulate the experiment with the working model and take the variance of \(\widehat\Psi_m\) across replications.

Bias depends only on the mean mix a video sees; variance depends on the whole joint draw.

Both terms are computed for the estimator being tuned, so the same calculation ranks estimators as well as designs.

Average RMSE across arms is the default loss; any other summary works. Curves are typically flat near the minimum, so read off the region, not the third decimal.

Design replay

Conditioning on the pilot estimates, simulate each candidate \(\bar\alpha\) and read off the estimator’s spread.

Steps 3 and 4 — Run, then validate

3. Main run

Fresh clusters at the tuned design, with a prespecified decision rule.

Where the precision pays: more arms screened, faster, with rankings you can act on.

4. Validation

A cluster-uniform experiment, on the selected arm(s) only.

Coverage for the GATE is generally not correct at interior designs, so the headline number comes from here.

Search, then claim.

  • Different stages in an experiment may have different bias-variance tradeoffs that make sense!

Main run: at the tuned design

  • 30 configurations over five continuous parameters
  • per-session Dirichlet draws were infeasible at scale, so a small library of quasi-random mixes, one per session
  • the variance reduction is what made the optimization loop workable
  • validated session-level: stalls down, nothing else degraded

Bias falls and variance rises along the dial

100 clusters × 50 units · three arms (control, high, low) · 1,000 replications

Difference-in-means with weak interference (\(c = 0.1\)). \(\rho_T = 1\): cluster-uniform; \(\rho_T = 0\): unit-level.

As \(\rho_u\) rises, the best design slides from nearly cluster-uniform to nearly unit-level.

Difference-in-means can beat the correct model

  • The linear model is correctly specified, and still loses to difference-in-means
    • it pays variance for every exposure slope it has to estimate (and there are many).

Bigger picture

  1. Pilot, tune, run, validate.
  • Different phases deserve different designs!
  • Offer-Westort: Explore-Confirm Designs for Testing Intervention Families
    • You can generate valid tests over multi-phase designs
  1. Research programs also benefit from thinking sequentially
  • Are we in an exploration phase or a validation phase?
  1. Experimentation is a powerful optimization tool
  • Dimmery: Social Science without Generalization
    • Internal validity is sufficient for many important problems
